66e2af306a.q: How much carbohydrate per hour do endurance athletes actually need according to exercise physiology research?
66e2af306a.a: For performances lasting under 90 minutes to 120 minutes, athletes typically have enough glycogen stores on board. However, once glycogen stores begin dropping significantly, supplementing carbohydrates becomes beneficial. For high-carb fueling exceeding 60 grams per hour, the glucose-to-fructose ratio becomes critical—traditionally a 2-to-1 ratio—because glucose transporters in the intestine can only move approximately 60 grams of glucose per hour from the intestine into the body.

6bebfbeac6.q: What is bonking in endurance exercise and what are its symptoms?
6bebfbeac6.a: Bonking occurs when blood glucose begins to drop significantly after liver glycogen stores can no longer maintain resting glucose levels. Athletes experience symptoms including lightheadedness, shaking, and hypoglycemia—essentially feeling very poor and unable to maintain pace. Bonking results from depleted muscle and liver glycogen, leaving insufficient glucose to fuel both the brain and working muscles, forcing athletes to slow dramatically or walk.

8b21f7a54f.q: Why do endurance athletes burn through carbohydrates faster than fat even though body fat stores are larger?
8b21f7a54f.a: The metabolic rate of energy extraction differs significantly between fuel sources. Fat oxidation is a much slower metabolic process for extracting ATP than carbohydrate metabolism. At harder intensities, the body cannot produce ATP from fat fast enough to meet energy demands, so it must rely increasingly on carbohydrates. The faster an athlete goes, the more carbohydrates are required, and since glycogen stores are finite, they deplete quickly at high intensity.

50234ecf41.q: What specific problem was CarbsFuel created to solve in the endurance sports fueling market?
50234ecf41.a: In the early 2020s, high-carbohydrate fueling recommendations of 90 to 120 grams per hour required athletes to consume four to six gel packets hourly at three to five dollars per packet, costing twenty to fifty dollars per hour of training. Co-founder Gabe was frustrated with the complexity and cost of achieving high-carb fueling. CarbsFuel was born from the idea of delivering 50 grams of carbohydrates for two dollars—a significantly more affordable and dense alternative to existing products.
